master-of-the-house-1925.gazette: Dreyer had a life-size apartment built inside the studio rather than assembled from flats — rooms in true proportion, doors that led somewhere, a kitchen that functioned. The camera could cross a threshold instead of cutting around it. The domestic tyranny in the film is measured out in floor plan.

the-general-1926.gazette: Keaton ran working locomotives on narrow-gauge track in Oregon, and staged the bridge collapse by taking a trestle out from under a moving engine. There was one take, because there was one engine. It lay in the riverbed for years afterward, until wartime scrap crews came for it.

meet-me-in-st-louis-1944.gazette: A row of houses went up on the Culver City backlot and stood in for a Missouri that had been gone forty years. The Louisiana Purchase Exposition itself was built to be temporary — staff and plaster, demolished within months of closing in 1904 — and was raised again in paint for the finale. The street outlasted the picture on the lot.
meet-me-in-st-louis-1944.prism: A fair designed to disappear got its permanent version from a studio. For a lot of people the 1904 Exposition now looks the way MGM decided it looked.

french-cancan-1955.gazette: Montmartre here is a sound stage; Renoir declined to shoot the quarter that was still standing outside. The Moulin Rouge opened in 1889, and the film rebuilds the milieu that produced it — the laundries, the dance halls, the crowd on the hill. The painters who recorded that quarter worked from life. Renoir worked from the paintings.

a-man-escaped-1956.gazette: André Devigny went over the wall of Montluc prison in Lyon in August 1943, hours before he was due to be shot. Bresson filmed inside Montluc with Devigny advising, and reproduced the method in order: the spoon worked into a chisel, the door panels loosened, rope spun from bedding and wire. Almost everything else is withheld except the work.

harakiri-1962.gazette: The film sets itself in 1630, in a Japan where abolished clans had put masterless samurai on the road in their thousands, without service or income. The ritual it stages is exact: the courtyard raked, the seconds placed, the white cloth, the order of who speaks and when. Every gesture is correct, and the correctness is what kills the man performing them.
harakiri-1962.prism: Nobody in the House of Ii breaks a rule, and a man still dies badly — protocol is the weapon. The chronicle the clan writes up afterward is accurate too, and it leaves out everything.

red-beard-1965.gazette: The Koishikawa clinic was built to work rather than to photograph, with Toho's carpenters finishing cabinetry the camera never opened. The shoot ran roughly two years, long enough that Mifune's beard was his own. It was the last of the sixteen films he and Kurosawa made together.

the-battle-of-algiers-1966.gazette: Saadi Yacef ran FLN operations in the Casbah during the 1957 battle, wrote the account the film was drawn from, and then played the part on the same streets. Pontecorvo shot in Algiers with a largely nonprofessional cast and used no newsreel — a claim the production had to spell out on the print itself. France kept the film off its own screens for years.

le-cercle-rouge-1970.gazette: The Place Vendôme job runs close to half an hour with nothing spoken. Melville worked it out as procedure — the alarm's weak point, the tools, the order of operations, the waiting — and shot it at the pace the work would actually take rather than the pace a scene usually takes. What holds the sequence together is the sequence.
le-cercle-rouge-1970.prism: Competence is the entire drama here, and the plan still doesn't save them. Melville's men come apart after the job, on the part nobody could rehearse.

the-godfather-part-ii-1974.gazette: Two periods were dressed at once: a 1900s Little Italy laid over East Sixth Street in Manhattan, and Batista's Havana on its last New Year's, staged in the Dominican Republic because Cuba was closed to the production. The Caribbean streets needed little alteration; the Manhattan ones needed a century removed. Both were being built by the same crew in the same year, half a century and a revolution apart.

barry-lyndon-1975.gazette: The interiors were shot by candlelight through a Zeiss f/0.7 originally made for NASA, a lens fast enough to take an image off three wicks. Houses were mostly real, and costumes were cut to period pattern, some of them from antique garments. Compositions were framed against the painters of the era, which is the standard the film invited.

days-of-heaven-1978.gazette: The wheat country is Alberta, standing in for the Texas Panhandle of 1916, and the machinery is real — steam tractors and threshers sourced in working order and run through an actual harvest. Almendros shot largely by available light in the last minutes before dark, which left only a narrow usable window each day. The house on the horizon was built for the film, with nothing behind it.
days-of-heaven-1978.prism: The sun set the call sheet: real machines and real light both dictated when anyone could work. Beauty that specific is a logistics problem before it is a style.

a-time-to-live-and-a-time-to-die-1985.gazette: Hou's family crossed from Guangdong to Taiwan in the late 1940s carrying what a one-year stay would require. The film rebuilds that household in Fengshan — the cheap bamboo furniture bought because nobody meant to stay, the grandmother still looking for the road back to the mainland. Hou speaks the opening narration himself and names the house as his own.

ran-1985.gazette: Kurosawa's crews spent years on the dressing alone: Sengoku armor and banners made by hand, cloth woven and dyed for the purpose. The castle that burns was a full-scale structure raised on the slopes of Mount Fuji and then genuinely set alight, with the shot available once. He had painted the entire film in advance, while waiting for someone to finance it.

empire-of-the-sun-1987.gazette: Ballard passed the last years of the war interned at Lunghua outside Shanghai, a boy separated from his parents in the camp system; the novel arrived nearly forty years on. Spielberg's unit was among the first Western productions allowed into Shanghai since 1949, and staged the 1941 panic on the Bund itself, on the street where it happened. Ballard visited the shoot and appears briefly in the party scene.
empire-of-the-sun-1987.prism: He was a child who found the war exciting, and wrote it that way — the book's real provocation is how much of a catastrophe a boy could enjoy. The film keeps that intact instead of correcting it.
